section_summary: This section concludes a detailed U.S. military intelligence estimate of Japan’s army, navy, mobilization capacity, equipment, doctrine, and strategic position as of 1939. Subsequent documents concern Japan’s laws protecting military-resource information, plans to shift military strength to the Asian continent, reported troop discontent and movements, and efforts to recruit South American aviators. The final two pages are a seemingly misfiled fragment of a July 1940 military attaché report on Japan’s jury system.

subfiles.title: Japan Combat Estimate (continued)
subfiles.to: United States military and government officials
subfiles.about: Continues a comprehensive intelligence estimate of Japan’s army, navy, mobilization system, combat doctrine, and strategic position.
subfiles.summary: The estimate catalogs Japanese individual and tactical equipment, chemical-warfare capacity, medical and transportation services, military schools, training, morale, recruitment, and conscription. It evaluates Japan’s ability to mobilize roughly sixty divisions while warning that shortages of equipment, ammunition, raw materials, gold, and foreign credit constrain further expansion. The naval section describes personnel, ships, aviation, fleet organization, bases, and readiness, while the conclusions emphasize Japan’s strong strategic position in East Asia and the western Pacific.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on G-2’s Japan Combat Estimate
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State files and officials
subfiles.about: Summarizes G-2 estimates of Japanese troop distribution, reserves, divisions, pilots, aircraft, and supply limitations.
subfiles.summary: Memo on G-2's estimate: 1.5 million Japanese under arms in January 1939; seven million trained reserve, but equipment limits mean no more than sixty divisions and difficulties if the USSR joins.

subfiles.title: Japan Combat Estimate, Changes No. 1
subfiles.to: Holders of the Japan Combat Estimate
subfiles.about: Lists numerical and textual corrections to the March 31, 1939 Japan Combat Estimate.
subfiles.summary: Correction sheet to the Japan Combat Estimate, changing figures such as 348,000 to 355,000 and deleting a word from the conclusion.

subfiles.title: Draft Law for Protection of Secrets Concerning Resources for Military Purposes
subfiles.doc_type: Naval intelligence attaché report with translated draft law
subfiles.from: U.S. Office of Naval Intelligence, based on Naval Attaché Tokyo reporting
subfiles.about: Translates and comments upon a proposed Japanese law broadly defining and protecting information about resources usable for military purposes.
subfiles.summary: The report warns that the proposed law, together with the Military Secrets Protection Law and National General Mobilization Law, would make ordinary commercial and industrial intelligence exceptionally difficult to collect. Its twenty-six articles cover production, stockpiles, imports, skilled personnel, transport, aerodromes, ships, communications, research, weather information, and concealment of facilities. It authorizes inspections and restrictions on access or photography and imposes prison terms and fines for collecting or disclosing protected information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 3778 on the National General Mobilization Law
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a despatch concerning progress toward invoking Japan’s National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Despatch No. 3778 (March 28, 1939) on the National General Mobilization Law is filed under 800.00/850.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3835
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State files and officials
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Embassy’s report on Japan’s Law for the Protection of Secrets of Resources for Military Use.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch No. 3835: the new law complements the Military Secrets Law, with penalties up to ten years, but may change little as useful information was already nearly unobtainable.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3835: Law for the Protection of Secrets of Resources for Military Use
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on the enactment, scope, enforcement, and probable effects of Japan’s new military-resource secrecy law.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 3835: an extremely broad supplement to the Military Secrets Law, enforced by police and gendarmerie, expected chiefly to make permanent the difficulty of collecting information.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Law No. 25, Law for the Protection of Secrets of Resources for Military Use
subfiles.from: Government of Japan; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Enclosed with Despatch No. 3835 to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the Embassy’s English translation of Japan’s enacted Law No. 25 governing secrecy surrounding personnel and material resources for military use.
subfiles.summary: The law authorizes the War and Navy ministers to designate as secret extensive information about production, munitions, stockpiles, imports, skilled workers, transport, aircraft, communications, research, weather, and strategic facilities. It permits concealment orders, access and photography restrictions, inspections, and limits on public registers. Its penal provisions punish collection or disclosure for foreign benefit, participation in espionage organizations, obstruction, and violations by individuals or juridical persons, with colonial administration delegated to authorized offices in Korea, Taiwan, and South Sakhalin.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Mukden Despatch No. 359
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State files and officials
subfiles.about: Summarizes reports that Japan intended to increase and shift its principal military strength to the Asian continent.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Mukden Despatch No. 359: the War Minister calls continental armament inevitable; the consul sees the Kwantung Army outlook and a warning that emigrants may be demoralized by life in China.

subfiles.title: Forwarding Letter Enclosing Despatch No. 359
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Mukden
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of Despatch No. 359, “Japanese Army to Settle on Continent,” previously sent to the American Embassy at Peiping.
subfiles.summary: Langdon encloses his same-day Despatch No. 359 to the Peiping Embassy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 359: Japanese Army to Settle on Continent
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consulate General, Mukden
subfiles.to: Willys R. Peck, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese statements advocating a permanent shift of the army’s main strength to the Asian continent.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 359: the War Minister advocates moving Japan's main force to the continent; Langdon says the Kwantung Army has controlled Army spirit since 1931; Yanagawa warns of settlers' assimilation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hankow Telegram No. 130
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting rumors of serious discontent among Japanese troops near Hankow.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hankow Telegram No. 130 (793.94/15085): unconfirmed reports of Japanese troop discontent and army countermeasures.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hankow Telegram No. 132
subfiles.about: References a follow-up telegram about reports that Japanese units in the Hankow area were refusing to fight.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hankow Telegram No. 132: refusal to fight called the most serious problem for local Japanese army authorities, reported with reserve.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 63 on the Taiwan Denka Kaisha Factories
subfiles.about: References a memorandum concerning a Philippine citizen’s attempt to visit Taiwan Denka Kaisha factories in Keelung.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 63 on an attempted visit to Taiwan Denka Kaisha factories by Philippine citizen Escarrilla.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Kobe’s Despatch of August 14, 1939
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State files and officials
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Kobe report that previously rejected young men were being reexamined for military service.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Japan appears to have lowered induction standards; reexamined men reportedly get three months' training in Japan before mainland deployment.

subfiles.title: Military Movements
subfiles.to: Eugene H. Dooman, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports renewed examinations of previously rejected men and less conspicuous troop, casualty, and wounded-soldier movements through Kobe.
subfiles.summary: About three thousand Kobe men previously found unfit were ordered to a new Sasayama examination under relaxed standards, with three months' training; troop movements shifted to early morning or late night.

subfiles.title: File No. 894.20 Enclosure Charge Slip
subfiles.about: Records an administrative charge or withdrawal associated with an enclosure in file 894.20.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip for file 894.20 enclosure, dated October 12, 1945; recipient illegible.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2975: Two Japanese Military Aviators Embarked at Yokohama for Trip Around South America
subfiles.about: Reports a claim that two Japanese military aviators had sailed from Yokohama to recruit South American pilots for the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2975: the Chinese Minister in Rio says two Japanese military aviators embarked at Yokohama to tour South America, allegedly to recruit aviators for the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Report No. 10,158: Japanese Jury System (fragment)
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Concludes a digest and commentary on juror qualifications, jury selection, and the constitutional basis of Japan’s jury system.
subfiles.summary: Report No. 10,158: Japanese juries had twelve men; selection and exclusion rules described; juries determine facts while judges retain verdict and sentencing authority.
